title: Introduction to Accounting
tagline: What accounting is, who uses it, the branches it has grown into, and the equation every transaction must keep balanced.

overview.intro: Accounting is the language a business uses to describe itself. It is the process of identifying, recording, classifying and summarising the transactions of an organisation and communicating the results to the people who need them. A trader may remember cash sales in her head for a week, but a growing business has hundreds of transactions a month, and memory cannot be audited. Accounting converts that stream of events into a small set of statements that an owner, a bank or a tax officer can read and rely on. This chapter builds the vocabulary and the logic on which every later unit rests: the accounting equation, the branches of accounting, and the cycle that turns day-to-day entries into final accounts.

learningOutcomes: Define accounting and state its essential characteristics.
List the objectives of accounting and classify its users as internal or external.
Distinguish financial, cost and management accounting by purpose and audience.
Apply the accounting equation to a sequence of transactions.
Describe the accounting cycle from transaction to final accounts.

learn.title: The meaning and nature of accounting

blocks.text: Accounting is often called the language of business because it reports what a business has done, owns and owes in a form that outsiders can understand. The American Accounting Association describes it as the process of identifying, measuring, recording and communicating the required information about economic events to interested users. Four words carry the whole definition. Identifying means choosing only those events that are transactions in monetary terms; the arrival of a delivery van is an accounting event, but a visit from a supplier is not. Measuring means putting a reliable rupee figure on the event. Recording means entering it chronologically in the books. Communicating means preparing statements that a non-accountant can read.

items.meaning: The business treated as separate from its owner, so the owner’s personal dealings are not mixed with the firm’s.
An event measurable in money that changes the financial position of the entity.
A fixed stretch of time, usually a year, for which results are reported.
Only events that can be expressed in money enter the accounting records.

items.text: Cash sale of goods worth ₹5,000 is recorded because it changes cash and sales.
items.note: A price rise in the market is not recorded: it is an economic fact but not yet a transaction.

items.text: Purchase of a machine worth ₹40,000 on credit is recorded though no cash moved.
items.note: Both sides of the equation change: assets rise by the machine and liabilities rise by what is owed.

blocks.text: Accounting exists to answer questions that owners, lenders and regulators cannot answer from memory. Its first objective is to keep a systematic record of all transactions, which removes dependence on memory and makes error tracing possible. The second is to ascertain the profit or loss of the business by matching the revenue of a period against the expenses incurred to earn it. The third is to show the financial position by stating what the business owns and owes on a particular day. The fourth is to provide information to interested parties: a bank deciding on a loan, a creditor deciding on credit terms and a government deciding on tax all read the same statements for different reasons.

items: Systematic record keeping: a chronological journal and a classified ledger replace recall.
Profit or loss: the trading and profit and loss account measures performance for a period.
Financial position: the balance sheet reports assets, liabilities and capital at a date.
Assistance to management: accounting data feeds budgets, costing and decision making.
Liquidity information: the cash position shows whether obligations can be met as they fall due.
Evidence in law: properly kept books are admissible evidence in disputes and in the winding up of a company.

blocks.caption: Objective of accounting and the statement that delivers it
rows: Trading and Profit and Loss Account
Did the period earn a profit?
What does the business own and owe?
Is this a safe party to deal with?

learn.title: Users of accounting information and the branches of accounting

blocks.text: Users fall into two groups. Internal users are inside the organisation: the proprietor, directors and managers who plan operations and compare results against targets. External users stand outside it: investors assessing a return, lenders assessing repayment capacity, suppliers deciding credit limits, customers checking continuity of supply, employees negotiating wages, and the government collecting taxes. The two groups differ in what they need. Managers want detailed, frequent and forward-looking figures, which the business keeps for itself. Outsiders want published, historical and audited figures on a comparable basis, which is why accounting standards exist.

blocks.caption: Users of accounting information
rows: Can this borrower service the loan?
Should we extend sixty days’ credit?
Should I buy or hold this share?
Has the correct tax been paid?
Can the firm sustain pay rises?

blocks.text: From these users grew three branches. Financial accounting produces the statutory statements for outsiders on a historical basis. Cost accounting ascertains the cost of each product, job or process so that pricing and control become possible. Management accounting turns both into internal reports: budgets, variance statements and cash forecasts that help managers choose between alternatives rather than merely report the past.

items: Financial accounting: historical, summarised, audited, published.
Cost accounting: unit and process costs, overhead absorption, work-in-progress valuation.
Management accounting: budgets, standard costing variances, cash forecasts, decision data.

learn.title: The accounting equation and the effect of transactions

blocks.text: Everything a business owns is called an asset, and every asset is funded either by an outside party (a liability) or by the owner (capital). This gives the accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Capital. Capital is the owner’s claim on the business, so it is often written as the residual that remains after liabilities are deducted from assets. Because every transaction has two sides, the equation stays in balance after each one. A cash purchase increases one asset and decreases another: total assets are unchanged. A credit purchase increases an asset and increases a liability: both sides rise by the same amount. An owner’s cash introduction increases assets and capital together.

blocks.caption: Effect of common transactions on the accounting equation
rows: Owner brings cash into the business
Assets and capital both rise by the same amount
Goods bought on credit from a supplier

items.text: Capital ₹2,00,000 and a computer bought for ₹50,000 cash give assets of ₹2,00,000 (cash ₹1,50,000 + computer ₹50,000) against capital of ₹2,00,000.
items.note: The equation holds because the purchase merely converted one asset into another.

items.text: Goods worth ₹30,000 are bought on credit and later ₹10,000 is paid in cash.
items.note: Assets change to stock ₹30,000 − cash ₹10,000 and liabilities fall to ₹20,000, so both sides remain equal.

blocks.text: The accounting cycle is the fixed sequence of steps that turns raw transactions into statements, and it repeats every accounting period. It begins with a transaction supported by a source document such as an invoice, a receipt or a pay-in slip. The transaction is entered in the journal in date order, posted to the ledger so that each account carries its own total, and at the end of the period the ledger balances are extracted into a trial balance to test arithmetic accuracy. Adjustments for accruals, prepaid expenses and depreciation are then made, final accounts are prepared, closing entries transfer the year’s nominal balances to capital, and the cycle starts again.

items: Source documents capture the evidence: invoice, receipt, pay-in slip, debit note.
Journal entry records the transaction chronologically with its debit and credit.
Ledger posting classifies the entry under the account it affects.
Trial balance extracts balances to test that total debits equal total credits.
Adjustments record accruals, prepayments, depreciation and bad debts.
Final accounts report profit and position, closing entries reset the nominal accounts.

blocks.text: The cycle matters because each stage is a check on the one before it. A journal that does not agree with its source document is caught at posting; a ledger that does not balance is caught in the trial balance; a trial balance that balances can still conceal a compensating error, which is why a reading of the final figures is the last safeguard.

keyPoints: Accounting is identifying, recording, classifying, summarising and communicating monetary transactions.
Only events measurable in money enter the records; non-monetary events are narrated in the records only when significant.
The business entity concept keeps the owner’s private dealings out of the firm’s accounts.
Objectives: records, profit or loss, financial position, information to interested parties.
Internal users are owners, directors and managers; external users include lenders, creditors, investors and government.
Financial accounting looks backward and is published; management accounting looks forward and is internal.
Assets = Liabilities + Capital, and every transaction preserves the balance.
A credit purchase raises assets and liabilities equally; a cash purchase merely swaps one asset for another.
The cycle runs source document → journal → ledger → trial balance → adjustments → final accounts → closing entries.
A trial balance proves arithmetic equality but cannot detect errors of principle or omission.
examFocus: Definition questions usually ask for the meaning of accounting plus four objectives; earn full marks by naming the statement that delivers each objective.
Equation questions give a sequence of transactions and ask for the closing position; show the effect line by line rather than only the final total.
Distinguish the three branches by their audience: outsiders, product costing, internal decisions.

vocabulary.meaning: Process of recording, classifying and summarising transactions and communicating results.
Owner’s claim on the business; the amount invested plus profits less drawings.
A resource owned by the business that carries a future economic benefit.
An amount owed by the business to an outside party.
The business treated as a person separate from its owner.
The repeating sequence of steps from transaction to final accounts.
The state of assets, liabilities and capital on a stated date.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best describes the accounting process?
questions.explanation: Accounting starts with identifying and recording transactions, classifies them into ledgers, summarises them into statements and then communicates them to users.

questions.prompt: A business buys goods worth ₹25,000 on credit. Which effect does the accounting equation show?
options: Assets rise by ₹25,000 and liabilities rise by ₹25,000
Assets rise by ₹25,000 and capital falls by ₹25,000
Only liabilities change; total assets stay the same
Capital rises by ₹25,000 and liabilities fall by ₹25,000
questions.answer: Assets rise by ₹25,000 and liabilities rise by ₹25,000
questions.explanation: Stock increases as an asset and the supplier becomes a creditor, so both sides of the equation increase by the identical amount.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an internal user of accounting information?
options: A bank assessing a loan application
The production manager planning next month’s output
A creditor fixing a credit limit
questions.answer: The production manager planning next month’s output
questions.explanation: Internal users belong to the organisation: owners, directors and managers. Banks, creditors and the government are outside parties.

questions.prompt: Which concept requires the business to be treated as distinct from its owner?
questions.explanation: The business entity concept separates the firm’s affairs from the owner’s personal affairs, so drawings are not treated as business expenses.
Every asset of the business is financed either by an outside party (liability) or by the owner (capital), so the two sides must always agree.

questions.prompt: The accounting statement that shows what a business owns and owes on one named day is the __________.
questions.explanation: The balance sheet is a position statement as at a date, unlike the profit and loss account which covers a period.

questions.prompt: State the meaning of accounting and mention any three of its essential characteristics.
questions.answer: Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording and communicating financial information about an entity to interested users. Its characteristics are that it deals only in monetary terms, it records transactions systematically and chronologically, and it reports the result to users in the form of statements.
questions.explanation: The definition marks are earned by naming the five activities; the characteristics show that the student understands what qualifies as an accounting event.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between financial accounting and management accounting on the basis of users and timing.
questions.answer: Financial accounting is prepared mainly for external users such as investors, lenders and the government; it is historical, summarised and published in statutory statements. Management accounting is prepared for internal managers; it is forward-looking, detailed and never published, covering budgets, forecasts and decision data.
questions.explanation: The two branches differ in audience and orientation: outsiders reading the past versus managers planning the future.

questions.prompt: Explain the accounting cycle with the help of a suitable example of a cash purchase.
questions.answer: The accounting cycle repeats every period: (1) a source document such as an invoice or cash memo evidences the transaction; (2) the transaction is journalised in date order; (3) it is posted to the ledger account it affects; (4) balances are extracted into a trial balance where total debits must equal total credits; (5) adjustments for accruals, prepayments and depreciation are recorded; (6) final accounts are prepared; (7) closing entries transfer nominal balances to capital. For a cash purchase of goods worth ₹10,000: the cash memo is the source document, the journal entry debits Purchases and credits Cash, the purchases account is increased in the ledger, ₹10,000 appears in the trial balance and finally in the trading account, and at year end the purchases balance is closed to trading account so the cycle can restart.
questions.explanation: The answer must show every stage of the cycle and then apply it to a single transaction, because the example is what proves the sequence is understood rather than memorised.

questions.prompt: On 1 April a proprietor started business with cash of ₹1,00,000, bought goods worth ₹40,000 on credit, paid rent of ₹6,000 and sold goods costing ₹15,000 for ₹20,000 cash. State the accounting equation after these transactions and comment on the profit.
questions.answer: Assets ₹1,39,000 = Liabilities ₹40,000 + Capital ₹99,000. Cash is 1,00,000 − 6,000 + 20,000 = ₹1,14,000 and stock is 40,000 − 15,000 = ₹25,000, so total assets are ₹1,39,000. Creditors stand at ₹40,000. Capital is the opening ₹1,00,000 adjusted by the results: a gross profit of ₹5,000 (20,000 − 15,000) less rent of ₹6,000 gives a net loss of ₹1,000, so capital closes at ₹99,000 and the equation holds.
questions.explanation: The student must track each transaction separately, then add profit or loss to capital; the rent payment reduces both cash and capital, which is the step most often missed.
